blocks.quote: The image is a matrix
blocks.section: The image is a matrix

blocks.quote: Take the simplest picture worth looking at: an **8×8 checkerboard**. It *is* an $8\times 8$ matrix of 0s and 1s:
blocks.section: The image is a matrix

blocks.quote: A checkerboard hides no texture, so every distortion shows: a shear leans the squares, a non-uniform scale turns them into rectangles, a rotation tilts them all.
blocks.section: The image is a matrix

blocks.quote: To warp an image by an affine map: for every output pixel $\mathbf{q}$, ask *which source pixel lands here?* The answer is $\mathbf{p} = A^{-1}\mathbf{q}$. This is **inverse mapping**: every output pixel gets exactly one value. (Forward mapping — pushing source pixels out — leaves holes.) When $\mathbf{p}$ falls between pixels: **nearest neighbour** (crisp 0/1) or **bilinear** (smooth 0-to-1 blend along seams).

blocks.quote: The first non-affine move
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: Every map so far with $\det M \neq 0$ is **one-to-one**: each output has at most one input. Nothing gets glued. Such maps are **homeomorphisms onto their image** — continuous, invertible, with a continuous inverse \cite[nLab, homeomorphism]{nlab_homeomorphism}; Morris's definition is exactly this — one-to-one, onto, with the topology preserved in both directions (\cite[Morris, Topology Without Tears, Ch. 4, p. 75]{morris2007topology}). By **Brouwer's invariance of domain** (~1910), any continuous one-to-one map of $\mathbb{R}^n$ onto its image is one, so this is the largest such family \cite[nLab, invariance of domain]{nlab_invariance_of_domain}. Their unbreakable rule:
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: > A homeomorphism cannot change the topology of space. Lines stay lines, holes stay holes, links stay linked.
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: The simplest map that breaks this rule is the **fold**:
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: The crease is the hyperplane $\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{p} = c$. Points on the near side ($\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{p} \le c$) are untouched. Points on the far side are pushed a distance $\lambda$ times their distance from the crease. One knob $\lambda$:
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: - $\lambda = 0$ — identity (still affine)
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: - $0 < \lambda < 1$ — bent, still one-to-one
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: - $\lambda = 1$ — far half flattened *onto* the crease (maximum overlap)
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: - $\lambda = 2$ — mirror in the crease (a paper fold)
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: - $\lambda > 2$ — overshoot; far side passes through near side
blocks.section: The first non-affine move

blocks.quote: Separating a ring with one fold
blocks.section: Separating a ring with one fold

blocks.quote: Now use the fold for something. The textbook problem that **no straight cut can solve**: a **circle inside a circle** — an inner disk, one class, and an outer annulus, the other. No line separates them: any line that misses the inner disk still cuts the outer annulus, so outer points always land on *both* sides.
blocks.section: Separating a ring with one fold

blocks.quote: That is the 2-D test case of the Origami chapter: **fold into unoccupied dimensions until a flat cut reaches the class that was surrounded** (\cite[Keup & Helias, 2022]{keup2022origami}). A ReLU fold does it in one piece; a **tanh** fold does it smoothly — no crease, the lift is a gentle S-curve that pushes right at the border of the flat part. And watch $\lambda = 2$: the mirror fold lands every lifted point back on the floor, and the gap closes again.
blocks.section: Separating a ring with one fold

blocks.quote: Unthreading a chain
blocks.section: Unthreading a chain

blocks.quote: The move no homeomorphism can do
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: Two rings threaded like a chain link — the **Hopf link** \cite[nLab, Hopf link]{nlab_hopf_link}\cite[Wikipedia, Hopf link]{hopf_link_wiki}. A **knot** is one closed loop; a **link** is several \cite[nLab, knot]{nlab_knot}\cite[nLab, link]{nlab_link}. The only legal way to move one link into another is an **ambient isotopy**: the whole space deformed continuously, one-to-one at every instant \cite[nLab, isotopy]{nlab_isotopy}. Two configurations connected by such a motion are the *same* link; the trivial state — two loops that are not linked — is the **unlink** \cite[nLab, unknot]{nlab_unknot}.
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: The Hopf link: two circles linked once, with linking number $\pm 1$. Every homeomorphism preserves that number, so no ambient isotopy can separate them; only a non-homeomorphic fold can. Image: \cite[Jim Belk]{hopf_link_image}, public domain.
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: The certificate that says the Hopf link *cannot* be unthreaded is a single integer, the **linking number** \cite[nLab, linking number]{nlab_linking_number}:
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: For the Hopf link it is $\pm 1$; for two unlinked circles it is $0$. The formula above is **Gauss's integral** over the two curves \cite[Wikipedia, linking number (Gauss integral)]{linking_number_wiki} — the lab below runs it live. Every homeomorphism preserves the number (it is a topological invariant \cite[nLab, topological property]{nlab_topological_property}\cite[Wikipedia, homeomorphism]{homeomorphism_wiki}), so *no* affine, projective, or Möbius motion can drop it from $1$ to $0$.
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: - **Montúfar, Pascanu, Cho & Bengio** — the piecewise-linear regions of a rectifier net tile the input space, and their count grows exponentially with depth (\cite[Montúfar et al., 2014]{montufar2014regions}). The full proof, including the lower bound showing the exponential growth is unavoidable, is in \citeauthor{petersen2024mathdl} (\citeyear{petersen2024mathdl}), Ch.\ 6.
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: - **Keup & Helias** — to make tangled classes separable, a network **folds the data manifold into unoccupied higher dimensions** until a flat cut reaches the "island" class another class surrounds (\cite[Keup & Helias, 2022]{keup2022origami}); their 2-D test case — a ring inside a ring — is the flat cousin of the chained rings above.
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: - **Amrami & Goldberg** — problems that need exponentially many parameters at any fixed depth are solved with zero error by a net of *linear* depth and width $\le 4$, via an explicit space-folding construction (\cite[Amrami & Goldberg, 2021]{amrami2021depth}).
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: - **Lewandowski et al.** — a straight input line arrives in activation space as a non-convex path (each crease loses convexity), and their space-folding measure grows with depth in well-trained nets (\cite[Lewandowski et al., 2025]{lewandowski2025spacefolds}).
blocks.section: The move no homeomorphism can do

blocks.quote: Four papers, one object: the piecewise-affine map that creases and overlaps space. The Origami chapter is the full treatment; this chapter hands you the geometry to play with.

blocks.quote: Group Structure: The Algebra of Symmetry
blocks.section: Group Structure: The Algebra of Symmetry

blocks.quote: | Axiom | Statement | Example in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ |
blocks.section: Group Structure: The Algebra of Symmetry

blocks.quote: | **Associativity** | $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$ | $(2+3)+4 = 2+(3+4) = 9 \pmod{12}$ |
blocks.section: Group Structure: The Algebra of Symmetry

blocks.quote: The simplest everyday example is **clock arithmetic**: the 12 hours form a group under addition mod 12. Going forward 5 hours then 9 hours is the same as going forward 2 hours ($5+9=14\equiv2\pmod{12}$). The identity is $+0$ hours, and the inverse of $+5$ is $+7$ (since $5+7\equiv0$). The first interactive below lets you explore this directly.
blocks.section: Group Structure: The Algebra of Symmetry

blocks.quote: The impossibility of solving the general quintic by radicals was proved by **Ruffini** (1799, incomplete) and **Abel** (1824) (\cite[Abel–Ruffini theorem]{abel_ruffini_wiki}). \citeauthor{galoisgroup} then gave the exact criterion: an equation is solvable by radicals if and only if the **symmetry group of its roots**, now known as the Galois group, possesses a specific internal architecture, categorized today as a **solvable group**. He was the first to use *groupe* in a technical sense, though group-like ideas had earlier roots in Lagrange, Ruffini and Cauchy. The same algebra that classifies solvable equations is the one that makes the rotation matrices of positional encoding compose so cleanly (see the Positional Embeddings lesson).
blocks.section: Group Structure: The Algebra of Symmetry

blocks.quote: Reading the Cayley Table
blocks.section: Reading the Cayley Table

blocks.quote: - **The trick:** append a $1$, and composing affine maps is just multiplying the $3\times 3$ / $4\times 4$ matrices — the arithmetic behind image warps, graphics, cameras, and every linear layer.
blocks.section: Reading the Cayley Table

blocks.quote: - **Two dials to read:** $|\det M|$ says how much area/volume survives; the last row says whether you are still affine at all.
blocks.section: Reading the Cayley Table

blocks.quote: - **The first non-affine move is a fold** — exactly a ReLU: bent for $\lambda>0$, overlapping for $\lambda>1$, and the only move that can unthread a chain. Fold, then move affinely.
